## Observed Facts
Data Scope: BGL, 2005-06-03 15:42:50 to 2006-01-04 08:00:05 (whole period, no time filter), level = FATAL, grouped by component [E1][E2].

There are 855,195 FATAL Log Entries in total, spread across 4 Components [E2]:

| Component | FATAL Log Entries | Share of FATAL |
|---|---|---|
| KERNEL | 626,450 [E2] | about 73% |
| APP | 228,536 [E2] | about 27% |
| LINKCARD | 206 [E2] | under 0.1% |
| MMCS | 3 [E2] | negligible |

KERNEL and APP together account for nearly all FATAL Log Entries. The shares are my own arithmetic from the counts in [E2]. These are counts of Log Entries, not incidents.

## Hypotheses
- A single repeating fault or a burst could be inflating the KERNEL and APP counts. BGL logs often repeat the same message many times, so the counts may reflect volume rather than the number of distinct problems.
- LINKCARD and MMCS have few FATAL Log Entries but may still matter. A hardware or control-system fault can be rare yet severe.

## Unknowns
- I haven't checked whether the FATAL Log Entries are evenly spread over the period or concentrated in a few spikes.
- I don't know which messages or nodes drive the KERNEL and APP counts.
- The logs can't tell me how many distinct incidents these Log Entries represent.

## Next Step
Run a monthly or daily trend of FATAL Log Entries for KERNEL and APP to see whether they recur steadily or come in bursts. Then run count_by node and alert_tag for KERNEL FATAL to find the dominant message or hardware location.
